title: Constructors, initializers, and required
hook: Construction is how you make an invalid object unrepresentable. Field initializers, constructors, primary constructors, object initializers, and required properties are one toolbox — not competing fashions.

sections.heading: Ordinary and chained constructors
sections.prose: Instance constructors run after field initializers. this(...) chains to another constructor on the same type; base(...) is module 05. Validate at the boundary: empty tenant ids and missing RabbitMQ routing keys should throw ArgumentException (module 06) rather than exist as half-built objects. Static constructors run once per type and are a deadlock magnet if they touch other types — keep them tiny.

sections.heading: Primary constructors and object initializers
sections.prose: C# 12 primary constructors put parameters on class Type(params). Those parameters are in scope for the body and field initializers; capture them into properties if they must outlive the constructor. Object initializers set accessible set or init properties after the constructor returns. They combine with constructors that take the required identity (message id) while leaving optional knobs (timeout) to the initializer.

snippets.label: Primary constructor, required, and initializer
snippets.explanation: exchange is captured from the primary constructor. RoutingKey is required in the object initializer. RetryCount has a default so callers may omit it.

sections.heading: required and struct default
sections.prose: required (C# 11) is a compiler check on object creation: skip a required property and the call does not compile, unless you use SetsRequiredMembers on a constructor that assigns them. Structs still have default(T), which zero-initializes fields and does not run your parameterless constructor. new Struct() runs a parameterless constructor if you wrote one; default does not. That split bites configuration structs deserialized from Redis or created in arrays.

interviewTakeaways: Primary constructors capture inputs; promote them to properties if they are part of the API.
required plus init is how you keep object initializers honest.
commonPitfalls: Using object initializers on mutable classes and then treating the object as a value snapshot.
Assuming new MyStruct() and default(MyStruct) are identical when a parameterless constructor exists.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS constructors can return a different object; C# constructors cannot replace this. JS has no required-property compiler check.
TS definite assignment (!) and required in types are compile-time only. C# required is still compile-time, but init accessors are real IL.
